plan.KONU:
Sub-themes: ''Local and international food culture and food festivals in the city''
Target Vocabulary in Use (with revisional vocabulary)
Vocabulary for food events and festivals
Nouns: A cuisine, traditional (food), international (food), street food, a (food) fair, an international/regional/ local dish, a feast.
Vocabulary for food items
Nouns: Ingredients, cream, sweetcorn (corn-AmE), cereal, yoghurt (yogurt-AmE), seafood, salmon, beef, duck, tuna, a mushroom, a pineapple, a coconut, aubergine (eggplant-AmE), spinach, vinegar herbs, courgette (zucchini-AmE).
Vocabulary for international dishes
Nouns: Turkish pizza (lahmacun), couscous, barbecue (barbeque-AmE), a lamb chop, a kebab (shish kebab), a stew, noodles, a curry, tacos, a falafel, an omelette (an omelet-AmE), a burger, a biscuit (cookie-AmE), pasta, dessert, soup. Adjectives: Spicy, salty, hot, sweet, sour, bitter, savoury (savory-AmE), juicy, creamy, tender, giant. Verbs: To taste, a stall, a (street) vendor, to crack (eggs), to stir
*National and religious days, festivals and celebrations
“29 October Republic Day”, “23 April National Sovereignty and Children’s Day”, “19 May Commemoration of Atatürk, Youth and Sports Day”, “15 July Democracy and National Unity Day”, “30 August Victory Day”, "Eid al- Fitr (Eid-al-Ramadan)", "Festival of Sacrifice (Eid-al-Adha)".
*
(Relevant language content and (communicative) activities related to these national and religious days, festivals and celebrations will be developed and integrated across all themes and in all appropriate sections wherever and whenever possible.)
*
Local Cultural, Social and Moral Considerations of the Theme
In this theme, specific examples, cases, situations, events, and practices reflecting Turkish social, cultural, and moral customs, traditions, and heritage will be included across all sub-topics. This consideration will be age-and-level appropriate and selected with the Turkish learners’ social and cultural context in mind. A table of contents for this section is provided in the introduction to the whole English Language Curriculum.
Target Language Grammatical in Use
-
The Simple Present Tense with “or”: (Is this a local or an international festival? This is a local festival in Türkiye.)
-
The Simple Present Tense with “Wh- question words”: (What festival is this? It is the Orange Festival.) (What do you cook at the Orange Festival? We cook/make orange jam at the Orange Festival.)
(Where is the Omelette Festival? It is in France. What do they cook? They cook omelette in a very big pan.) (What are the ingredients? The ingredients are eggs, milk, cheese, green peppers and mushrooms.)
(How do they cook it? They put some milk, some eggs, and some mushrooms in a pan, they stir it and cook it.)
-
The Present Progressive Tense: (What are you cooking now? We are cooking orange cake now.)
-
The Simple Present Tense vs the Present Progressive Tense: (How do they serve it? They serve it with salad and bread but we’re/are serving it with green pepper now.)
Functions of Target Language Grammar in Use
-
Use of “Or”: Asking for options to help someone choose something by using the word “or”.
-
Use of the Simple Present Tense: Describing habits, routines, regular and repeated actions.
-
Use of the Present Progressive Tense: describing actions happening at or around the time of speaking.
-
Use of “Wh-questions”: Asking and answering about factual information in the present time with Wh- questions and with the pronouns we/you/they by using the Present Simple Tense and Present Progressive Tense.
-
Use of the Simple Present Tense vs the Present Progressive Tense: Comparing the descriptions of general truths, routines and habits by using the Simple Present Tense with actions happening at the present moment and/or around the current time by using the Present Progressive Tense.
Target Social Language Expressions in Use
This tastes amazing!
What a delicious meal!
I’m full, but I can’t stop eating! You’re/ are good at/bad at cooking!
Target Phonological Sounds in Use
Vowels: u: (/u/, /u:/)
Consonants: t: (/t/, /ð/, /θ/); v: (/v/)
*
(Phonetic symbols will not be taught. Only sounds will be practised through the target words in the theme.)
Sub-themes: ''Nature, endangered animals, their natural living conditions and habitats, and protection of them"
Vocabulary for endangered animals
Nouns: A polar bear, a sea turtle, an Asian elephant, a tiger, a whale, a great white shark, a penguin, a panda, a dolphin, a chimpanzee, a cheetah.
Vocabulary for their habitats
Nouns: Grasslands, rainforests, woodlands, jungles, oceans, deserts. Verbs: To need, to survive, to lessen, to breed, to hunt, to hide, to donate, to save, to protect, to produce, to prevent, to threaten, to reduce, to be at risk, to support, to affect.
Other related vocabulary
Nouns: A shelter, a disease, a food source, wildlife, volunteer, overhunting, overfishing, sea/marine pollution, air pollution, habitat loss, safety, population, survival, existence. Adjectives: dedicated, renewable, illegal.
Target Grammatical Structures in Use
-The Simple Present Tense
(Which animals are endangered? Leopards, cheetahs, elephants etc. are endangered animals.) (Where do endangered animals live? They live in their habitats.)
(What are their habitats? Their habitats are oceans, deserts, woodlands etc.)
(What are the reasons for their endangerment? Overhunting, water pollution, etc. are the reasons for their endangerment.)
-
The Simple Past Tense with Verb “To be”: Was/were; there was/there were (Affirmative, negative, and question forms):
(What was the population of the leopards in the past? There were about 700.000 leopards in the world 50 years ago.) (What is the population of the leopard now? -There are about 250.000 leopards in the world today.) (What was the main habitat of leopards/elephants etc..? Their main habitat was the jungle.)
(Where were the habitats of elephants? Their habitats were woodlands and forests.)
(What were the habitats of endangered animals like 50 years ago? They were cleaner and safer etc. than they are today.)
-
Use of “should” as a modal verb: (What should we do to protect endangered animals? We should protect their habitats. We should reduce water/air pollution. We should create safe areas for them.)
Functions of the Target Grammatical Structures in Use
-
Use of the Simple Present Tense: Describing facts, situations, and conditions in the past.
-
Use of the Simple Past Tense “Verb to be (Was/were)”: Asking and answering for information at a specific time in the past.
-
Use of the Simple Past Tense “There was/There were”: Asking and answering about factual information and questioning the existence of things, people, and animals at a specific time in the past.
-
Use of the modal “Should”: Describing advice, recommendation (and expectation), describing obligation (and expectation).

Spread the word!

EK_ALANLAR.Ölçme:
PERFORMANCE ASSIGNMENT
Students prepare a self-recording (visual, audio) at school/ at home, conducting an interview with classmates about ''local and international festivals which are held in the city, different kinds of food produced for such festivals, and local and international food culture'' and present it to the class and receiving feedback about it. They can also write and design the content of a ''food festival'' programme content and then they present and apply it as an acting out activity by inviting other students as visitors or food presenters to the festival in class to present different food cultures, cuisines, dishes etc. The assignment will be evaluated by using rubrics.
PERFORMANCE ASSIGNMENT
Students prepare a self-recording (visual, audio) at school/ at home, conducting an interview with classmates about ''endangered animals and their habitats and living conditions including where and how they live today and in the past, and ways to protect them from extinction'' and present it to the class and receiving feedback about it. They write and design the content of a documentary film script and then they present and apply it as a film-showing event in class by inviting other students as protectors, activists, or people who give harm to endangered animals. The assignment will be evaluated by using rubrics.
EK_ALANLAR.Farklılaştırma:
Expansion
Objective: To talk about different kinds of food produced for local and international festivals and food culture in English by using target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 1: Festival Organisers and Visitors Role-Play
The teacher divides students into two groups: Festival Organisers and Visitors. Each organiser group is assigned a specific festival (e.g., Adana Orange Flower Festival, French Omelette Festival, Spanish Taco Festival) and prepares key information, such as the festival’s location, food served, and activities. Organisers set up a ''festival booth'' to promote their event, while visitor groups rotate among the booths, asking questions like, ''What kind of food do you serve?'', ''What are you making/cooking?'' or ''Is this a local or international festival?''. Organisers respond fluently, using target vocabulary and language functions. After one round, the groups switch roles, so all students practise both presenting and questioning skills. The teacher and students provide feedback on vocabulary use and pronunciation. At the end of the activity, students prepare a poster about the festival they presented and display it on the class notice board. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.
Objective: To describe local and international food festivals and food culture in English by using target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 2: Festival Information Gap-Fill Listening Activity
The teacher prepares short audio clips describing different festivals and foods (e.g., ''In Japan, the Ramen Festival offers a variety of noodle dishes. Chefs prepare bowls of ramen with broth, vegetables, and chicken, and egg toppings'') and upload them to a web tool to create a listening gap-fill exercise. Students listen to the audio clips and complete the missing information directly on the web tool (e.g., ''The Festival offers a variety of noodle dishes''). They then record themselves using an audio recording tool, repeating the sentences fluently. The teacher plays some of the recordings in class and provides feedback on pronunciation and sentence accuracy, while students also give peer feedback to improve their speaking skills. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.
Supporting
Objective: To describe different kinds of food produced for local and international festivals and food culture in English by using target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 1: Festival Food Matching Game
The teacher gives students cards in two different categories: food items in the first category and festivals in the second. Students work in pairs, and each pair receives the cards. They match each food with the relevant festival. (e.g., Adana Orange Flower Festival – orange jam) After completing the matching, students create simple sentences based on examples shown on the board, such as: ''This is a local festival. They make orange jam at the Adana Orange Flower Festival''. The teacher encourages students to say their sentences aloud, helping them practise pronunciation. The pair that completes the correct matches the fastest and creates accurate sentences wins the activity. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.
Objective: To help students recognise and identify local and international festivals and food culture in English by using target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 2: Festival Food Listening Activity
The teacher prepares short audio clips describing different festivals and food (e.g., ''In France, at the Omelette Festival, they cook a large omelette in a big pan'') and uploads them to a web tool to create a listening quiz. Students listen to the audio clips and select the correct answer from multiple-choice options with the corresponding festival or food item (e.g., Omelette Festival – Omelette). After completing the listening part, students work in pairs to practise the sentences from the audio and record themselves using an audio recording tool, repeating the target sentences. The teacher plays some of the recordings and provides feedback on pronunciation and sentence accuracy, while students also give peer feedback. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.
Objective: To talk about endangered animals and conservation efforts in English by using the target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 1: Digital Role-Play: Save an Endangered Animal
Students work in small groups and choose or are assigned an endangered animal (e.g., (Antalya) Caretta caretta turtles or Anatolian leopards). Using a web tool, they create a digital character or visual story that introduces the animal, its habitat, and the problems it faces (such as pollution or habitat loss). The animal ''speaks'' using recorded audio or text-to-speech to describe its challenges and suggest solutions. Groups present their digital work to the class while others take notes and give feedback on vocabulary, fluency, and presentation skills. After all presentations, the class holds a brainstorming session to discuss ideas for protecting the animals, using phrases like ''Every little bit helps!'' and ''We need to act now!''. The teacher provides feedback on the presentations, and students finish with a clear plan of actions and solutions. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.
Objective: To identify endangered animals and conservation efforts in English by using the target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 2: Collaborative Reading Puzzle: Endangered Animals
The teacher divides a complex reading text about endangered animals (e.g., caretta caretta turtles, Anatolian leopards) into sections, each with unique information (like habitat, threats, or solutions). Students work in small groups, and each group reads one section, identifying key points and preparing questions about missing information they need from other groups. After reading, groups take turns asking and answering questions to complete the full picture of the topic (e.g., ''What is threatening the Anatolian leopard?''). Once they gather all the information, each group presents a summary of their findings, combining what they read and learned from others. The class ends with a discussion on solutions to protect endangered animals. The teacher gives feedback on reading comprehension, vocabulary use, and collaboration throughout the activity. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.
Objective: To describe endangered animals, their habitats, and ways to protect them from extinction in English by using the target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 1: Endangered Animal Habitat Matching Game
The teacher provides students with two sets of cards: one set with endangered animals (e.g., polar bear, sea turtle) and another with habitats (e.g., ocean, rainforest). Students work in pairs to match the animals with their correct habitats (e.g., Polar bear-Arctic). Once matched, they create simple sentences following the models on the board, such as ''A polar bear lives in the ocean'' or ''A tiger lives in the jungle'', and practice saying them aloud to improve pronunciation. The pair that completes the matches and sentences correctly and the fastest wins the game. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.
Objective: To identify endangered animals and their habitats in English by using target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 2: Endangered Animals Gap-Fill and Pronunciation Practice
The teacher starts by providing a short reading or audio about endangered animals like (Antalya) Caretta caretta sea turtles or Anatolian leopards. Students learn about their habitats, challenges, and ways to protect them. Afterward, students use the Web 2.00 tool to complete a gap-fill exercise with sentences such as ''A Caretta caretta turtle lays eggs on the (Mediterranean coast)''. After completing the exercise, students read their sentences aloud to practise pronunciation. The teacher then provides feedback on their accuracy and fluency.
The activity ends with a class discussion on protecting animals, using phrases like ''Every little bit helps!'' and ''It’s not too late to act!''. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.

plan.ÜNİTE: THEME 7: LIFE IN THE WORLD & NATURE
plan.KONU:
Sub-themes: ''Nature, endangered animals, their natural living conditions and habitats, and protection of them"
Target Vocabulary in Use (with revisional vocabulary)
Vocabulary for endangered animals
Nouns: A polar bear, a sea turtle, an Asian elephant, a tiger, a whale, a great white shark, a penguin, a panda, a dolphin, a chimpanzee, a cheetah.
Vocabulary for their habitats
Nouns: Grasslands, rainforests, woodlands, jungles, oceans, deserts. Verbs: To need, to survive, to lessen, to breed, to hunt, to hide, to donate, to save, to protect, to produce, to prevent, to threaten, to reduce, to be at risk, to support, to affect.
Other related vocabulary
Nouns: A shelter, a disease, a food source, wildlife, volunteer, overhunting, overfishing, sea/marine pollution, air pollution, habitat loss, safety, population, survival, existence. Adjectives: dedicated, renewable, illegal.
*National and religious days, festivals and celebrations
“29 October Republic Day”, “23 April National Sovereignty and Children’s Day”, “19 May Commemoration of Atatürk, Youth and Sports Day”, “15 July Democracy and National Unity Day”, “30 August Victory Day”, "Eid al- Fitr (Eid-al-Ramadan)", "Festival of Sacrifice (Eid-al-Adha)".
*
(Relevant language content and (communicative) activities related to these national and religious days, festivals and celebrations will be developed and integrated across all themes and in all appropriate sections wherever and whenever possible.)
*
Local Cultural, Social and Moral Considerations of the Theme
In this theme, specific examples, cases, situations, events, and practices reflecting Turkish social, cultural, and moral customs, traditions, and heritage will be included across all sub-topics. This consideration will be age-and-level appropriate and selected with the Turkish learners’ social and cultural context in mind. A table of contents for this section is provided in the introduction to the whole English Language Curriculum.
Target Grammatical Structures in Use
-The Simple Present Tense
(Which animals are endangered? Leopards, cheetahs, elephants etc. are endangered animals.) (Where do endangered animals live? They live in their habitats.)
(What are their habitats? Their habitats are oceans, deserts, woodlands etc.)
(What are the reasons for their endangerment? Overhunting, water pollution, etc. are the reasons for their endangerment.)
-
The Simple Past Tense with Verb “To be”: Was/were; there was/there were (Affirmative, negative, and question forms):
(What was the population of the leopards in the past? There were about 700.000 leopards in the world 50 years ago.) (What is the population of the leopard now? -There are about 250.000 leopards in the world today.) (What was the main habitat of leopards/elephants etc..? Their main habitat was the jungle.)
(Where were the habitats of elephants? Their habitats were woodlands and forests.)
(What were the habitats of endangered animals like 50 years ago? They were cleaner and safer etc. than they are today.)
-
Use of “should” as a modal verb: (What should we do to protect endangered animals? We should protect their habitats. We should reduce water/air pollution. We should create safe areas for them.)
Functions of the Target Grammatical Structures in Use
-
Use of the Simple Present Tense: Describing facts, situations, and conditions in the past.
-
Use of the Simple Past Tense “Verb to be (Was/were)”: Asking and answering for information at a specific time in the past.
-
Use of the Simple Past Tense “There was/There were”: Asking and answering about factual information and questioning the existence of things, people, and animals at a specific time in the past.
-
Use of the modal “Should”: Describing advice, recommendation (and expectation), describing obligation (and expectation).
Target Social Language Expressions in Use
It’s too late! / It’s not too late! Every little bit helps!
Spread the word!
In safe hands!
Target Phonological Sounds in Use
Diphthongs: ea: (/eə/), ee: /ɪə/ Consonants: w: (/w/); x: (/ks/)
*
(Phonetic symbols will not be taught. Only sounds will be practised through the target words in the theme.)

EK_ALANLAR.Ölçme:
PERFORMANCE ASSIGNMENT
Students prepare a self-recording (visual, audio) at school/ at home, conducting an interview with classmates about ''endangered animals and their habitats and living conditions including where and how they live today and in the past, and ways to protect them from extinction'' and present it to the class and receiving feedback about it. They write and design the content of a documentary film script and then they present and apply it as a film-showing event in class by inviting other students as protectors, activists, or people who give harm to endangered animals. The assignment will be evaluated by using rubrics.
EK_ALANLAR.Farklılaştırma:
Expansion
Objective: To talk about endangered animals and conservation efforts in English by using the target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 1: Digital Role-Play: Save an Endangered Animal
Students work in small groups and choose or are assigned an endangered animal (e.g., (Antalya) Caretta caretta turtles or Anatolian leopards). Using a web tool, they create a digital character or visual story that introduces the animal, its habitat, and the problems it faces (such as pollution or habitat loss). The animal ''speaks'' using recorded audio or text-to-speech to describe its challenges and suggest solutions. Groups present their digital work to the class while others take notes and give feedback on vocabulary, fluency, and presentation skills. After all presentations, the class holds a brainstorming session to discuss ideas for protecting the animals, using phrases like ''Every little bit helps!'' and ''We need to act now!''. The teacher provides feedback on the presentations, and students finish with a clear plan of actions and solutions. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.
Objective: To identify endangered animals and conservation efforts in English by using the target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 2: Collaborative Reading Puzzle: Endangered Animals
The teacher divides a complex reading text about endangered animals (e.g., caretta caretta turtles, Anatolian leopards) into sections, each with unique information (like habitat, threats, or solutions). Students work in small groups, and each group reads one section, identifying key points and preparing questions about missing information they need from other groups. After reading, groups take turns asking and answering questions to complete the full picture of the topic (e.g., ''What is threatening the Anatolian leopard?''). Once they gather all the information, each group presents a summary of their findings, combining what they read and learned from others. The class ends with a discussion on solutions to protect endangered animals. The teacher gives feedback on reading comprehension, vocabulary use, and collaboration throughout the activity. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.
Supporting
Objective: To describe endangered animals, their habitats, and ways to protect them from extinction in English by using the target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 1: Endangered Animal Habitat Matching Game
The teacher provides students with two sets of cards: one set with endangered animals (e.g., polar bear, sea turtle) and another with habitats (e.g., ocean, rainforest). Students work in pairs to match the animals with their correct habitats (e.g., Polar bear-Arctic). Once matched, they create simple sentences following the models on the board, such as ''A polar bear lives in the ocean'' or ''A tiger lives in the jungle'', and practice saying them aloud to improve pronunciation. The pair that completes the matches and sentences correctly and the fastest wins the game. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.
Objective: To identify endangered animals and their habitats in English by using target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 2: Endangered Animals Gap-Fill and Pronunciation Practice
The teacher starts by providing a short reading or audio about endangered animals like (Antalya) Caretta caretta sea turtles or Anatolian leopards. Students learn about their habitats, challenges, and ways to protect them. Afterward, students use the Web 2.00 tool to complete a gap-fill exercise with sentences such as ''A Caretta caretta turtle lays eggs on the (Mediterranean coast)''. After completing the exercise, students read their sentences aloud to practise pronunciation. The teacher then provides feedback on their accuracy and fluency.
The activity ends with a class discussion on protecting animals, using phrases like ''Every little bit helps!'' and ''It’s not too late to act!''. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.

plan.ÜNİTE: THEME 7: LIFE IN THE WORLD & NATURE
plan.KONU:
Sub-themes: ''Nature, endangered animals, their natural living conditions and habitats, and protection of them"
Target Vocabulary in Use (with revisional vocabulary)
Vocabulary for endangered animals
Nouns: A polar bear, a sea turtle, an Asian elephant, a tiger, a whale, a great white shark, a penguin, a panda, a dolphin, a chimpanzee, a cheetah.
Vocabulary for their habitats
Nouns: Grasslands, rainforests, woodlands, jungles, oceans, deserts. Verbs: To need, to survive, to lessen, to breed, to hunt, to hide, to donate, to save, to protect, to produce, to prevent, to threaten, to reduce, to be at risk, to support, to affect.
Other related vocabulary
Nouns: A shelter, a disease, a food source, wildlife, volunteer, overhunting, overfishing, sea/marine pollution, air pollution, habitat loss, safety, population, survival, existence. Adjectives: dedicated, renewable, illegal.
*National and religious days, festivals and celebrations
“29 October Republic Day”, “23 April National Sovereignty and Children’s Day”, “19 May Commemoration of Atatürk, Youth and Sports Day”, “15 July Democracy and National Unity Day”, “30 August Victory Day”, "Eid al- Fitr (Eid-al-Ramadan)", "Festival of Sacrifice (Eid-al-Adha)".
*
(Relevant language content and (communicative) activities related to these national and religious days, festivals and celebrations will be developed and integrated across all themes and in all appropriate sections wherever and whenever possible.)
*
Local Cultural, Social and Moral Considerations of the Theme
In this theme, specific examples, cases, situations, events, and practices reflecting Turkish social, cultural, and moral customs, traditions, and heritage will be included across all sub-topics. This consideration will be age-and-level appropriate and selected with the Turkish learners’ social and cultural context in mind. A table of contents for this section is provided in the introduction to the whole English Language Curriculum.
Target Grammatical Structures in Use
-The Simple Present Tense
(Which animals are endangered? Leopards, cheetahs, elephants etc. are endangered animals.) (Where do endangered animals live? They live in their habitats.)
(What are their habitats? Their habitats are oceans, deserts, woodlands etc.)
(What are the reasons for their endangerment? Overhunting, water pollution, etc. are the reasons for their endangerment.)
-
The Simple Past Tense with Verb “To be”: Was/were; there was/there were (Affirmative, negative, and question forms):
(What was the population of the leopards in the past? There were about 700.000 leopards in the world 50 years ago.) (What is the population of the leopard now? -There are about 250.000 leopards in the world today.) (What was the main habitat of leopards/elephants etc..? Their main habitat was the jungle.)
(Where were the habitats of elephants? Their habitats were woodlands and forests.)
(What were the habitats of endangered animals like 50 years ago? They were cleaner and safer etc. than they are today.)
-
Use of “should” as a modal verb: (What should we do to protect endangered animals? We should protect their habitats. We should reduce water/air pollution. We should create safe areas for them.)
Functions of the Target Grammatical Structures in Use
-
Use of the Simple Present Tense: Describing facts, situations, and conditions in the past.
-
Use of the Simple Past Tense “Verb to be (Was/were)”: Asking and answering for information at a specific time in the past.
-
Use of the Simple Past Tense “There was/There were”: Asking and answering about factual information and questioning the existence of things, people, and animals at a specific time in the past.
-
Use of the modal “Should”: Describing advice, recommendation (and expectation), describing obligation (and expectation).
Target Social Language Expressions in Use
It’s too late! / It’s not too late! Every little bit helps!
Spread the word!
In safe hands!
Target Phonological Sounds in Use
Diphthongs: ea: (/eə/), ee: /ɪə/ Consonants: w: (/w/); x: (/ks/)
*
(Phonetic symbols will not be taught. Only sounds will be practised through the target words in the theme.)

EK_ALANLAR.Ölçme:
PERFORMANCE ASSIGNMENT
Students prepare a self-recording (visual, audio) at school/ at home, conducting an interview with classmates about ''endangered animals and their habitats and living conditions including where and how they live today and in the past, and ways to protect them from extinction'' and present it to the class and receiving feedback about it. They write and design the content of a documentary film script and then they present and apply it as a film-showing event in class by inviting other students as protectors, activists, or people who give harm to endangered animals. The assignment will be evaluated by using rubrics.
EK_ALANLAR.Farklılaştırma:
Expansion
Objective: To talk about endangered animals and conservation efforts in English by using the target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 1: Digital Role-Play: Save an Endangered Animal
Students work in small groups and choose or are assigned an endangered animal (e.g., (Antalya) Caretta caretta turtles or Anatolian leopards). Using a web tool, they create a digital character or visual story that introduces the animal, its habitat, and the problems it faces (such as pollution or habitat loss). The animal ''speaks'' using recorded audio or text-to-speech to describe its challenges and suggest solutions. Groups present their digital work to the class while others take notes and give feedback on vocabulary, fluency, and presentation skills. After all presentations, the class holds a brainstorming session to discuss ideas for protecting the animals, using phrases like ''Every little bit helps!'' and ''We need to act now!''. The teacher provides feedback on the presentations, and students finish with a clear plan of actions and solutions. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.
Objective: To identify endangered animals and conservation efforts in English by using the target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 2: Collaborative Reading Puzzle: Endangered Animals
The teacher divides a complex reading text about endangered animals (e.g., caretta caretta turtles, Anatolian leopards) into sections, each with unique information (like habitat, threats, or solutions). Students work in small groups, and each group reads one section, identifying key points and preparing questions about missing information they need from other groups. After reading, groups take turns asking and answering questions to complete the full picture of the topic (e.g., ''What is threatening the Anatolian leopard?''). Once they gather all the information, each group presents a summary of their findings, combining what they read and learned from others. The class ends with a discussion on solutions to protect endangered animals. The teacher gives feedback on reading comprehension, vocabulary use, and collaboration throughout the activity. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.
Supporting
Objective: To describe endangered animals, their habitats, and ways to protect them from extinction in English by using the target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 1: Endangered Animal Habitat Matching Game
The teacher provides students with two sets of cards: one set with endangered animals (e.g., polar bear, sea turtle) and another with habitats (e.g., ocean, rainforest). Students work in pairs to match the animals with their correct habitats (e.g., Polar bear-Arctic). Once matched, they create simple sentences following the models on the board, such as ''A polar bear lives in the ocean'' or ''A tiger lives in the jungle'', and practice saying them aloud to improve pronunciation. The pair that completes the matches and sentences correctly and the fastest wins the game. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.
Objective: To identify endangered animals and their habitats in English by using target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 2: Endangered Animals Gap-Fill and Pronunciation Practice
The teacher starts by providing a short reading or audio about endangered animals like (Antalya) Caretta caretta sea turtles or Anatolian leopards. Students learn about their habitats, challenges, and ways to protect them. Afterward, students use the Web 2.00 tool to complete a gap-fill exercise with sentences such as ''A Caretta caretta turtle lays eggs on the (Mediterranean coast)''. After completing the exercise, students read their sentences aloud to practise pronunciation. The teacher then provides feedback on their accuracy and fluency.
The activity ends with a class discussion on protecting animals, using phrases like ''Every little bit helps!'' and ''It’s not too late to act!''. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.

plan.ÜNİTE: THEME 7: LIFE IN THE WORLD & NATURE
plan.KONU:
Sub-themes: ''Nature, endangered animals, their natural living conditions and habitats, and protection of them"
Target Vocabulary in Use (with revisional vocabulary)
Vocabulary for endangered animals
Nouns: A polar bear, a sea turtle, an Asian elephant, a tiger, a whale, a great white shark, a penguin, a panda, a dolphin, a chimpanzee, a cheetah.
Vocabulary for their habitats
Nouns: Grasslands, rainforests, woodlands, jungles, oceans, deserts. Verbs: To need, to survive, to lessen, to breed, to hunt, to hide, to donate, to save, to protect, to produce, to prevent, to threaten, to reduce, to be at risk, to support, to affect.
Other related vocabulary
Nouns: A shelter, a disease, a food source, wildlife, volunteer, overhunting, overfishing, sea/marine pollution, air pollution, habitat loss, safety, population, survival, existence. Adjectives: dedicated, renewable, illegal.
*National and religious days, festivals and celebrations
“29 October Republic Day”, “23 April National Sovereignty and Children’s Day”, “19 May Commemoration of Atatürk, Youth and Sports Day”, “15 July Democracy and National Unity Day”, “30 August Victory Day”, "Eid al- Fitr (Eid-al-Ramadan)", "Festival of Sacrifice (Eid-al-Adha)".
*
(Relevant language content and (communicative) activities related to these national and religious days, festivals and celebrations will be developed and integrated across all themes and in all appropriate sections wherever and whenever possible.)
*
Local Cultural, Social and Moral Considerations of the Theme
In this theme, specific examples, cases, situations, events, and practices reflecting Turkish social, cultural, and moral customs, traditions, and heritage will be included across all sub-topics. This consideration will be age-and-level appropriate and selected with the Turkish learners’ social and cultural context in mind. A table of contents for this section is provided in the introduction to the whole English Language Curriculum.
Target Grammatical Structures in Use
-The Simple Present Tense
(Which animals are endangered? Leopards, cheetahs, elephants etc. are endangered animals.) (Where do endangered animals live? They live in their habitats.)
(What are their habitats? Their habitats are oceans, deserts, woodlands etc.)
(What are the reasons for their endangerment? Overhunting, water pollution, etc. are the reasons for their endangerment.)
-
The Simple Past Tense with Verb “To be”: Was/were; there was/there were (Affirmative, negative, and question forms):
(What was the population of the leopards in the past? There were about 700.000 leopards in the world 50 years ago.) (What is the population of the leopard now? -There are about 250.000 leopards in the world today.) (What was the main habitat of leopards/elephants etc..? Their main habitat was the jungle.)
(Where were the habitats of elephants? Their habitats were woodlands and forests.)
(What were the habitats of endangered animals like 50 years ago? They were cleaner and safer etc. than they are today.)
-
Use of “should” as a modal verb: (What should we do to protect endangered animals? We should protect their habitats. We should reduce water/air pollution. We should create safe areas for them.)
Functions of the Target Grammatical Structures in Use
-
Use of the Simple Present Tense: Describing facts, situations, and conditions in the past.
-
Use of the Simple Past Tense “Verb to be (Was/were)”: Asking and answering for information at a specific time in the past.
-
Use of the Simple Past Tense “There was/There were”: Asking and answering about factual information and questioning the existence of things, people, and animals at a specific time in the past.
-
Use of the modal “Should”: Describing advice, recommendation (and expectation), describing obligation (and expectation).
Target Social Language Expressions in Use
It’s too late! / It’s not too late! Every little bit helps!
Spread the word!
In safe hands!
Target Phonological Sounds in Use
Diphthongs: ea: (/eə/), ee: /ɪə/ Consonants: w: (/w/); x: (/ks/)
*
(Phonetic symbols will not be taught. Only sounds will be practised through the target words in the theme.)

EK_ALANLAR.Ölçme:
PERFORMANCE ASSIGNMENT
Students prepare a self-recording (visual, audio) at school/ at home, conducting an interview with classmates about ''endangered animals and their habitats and living conditions including where and how they live today and in the past, and ways to protect them from extinction'' and present it to the class and receiving feedback about it. They write and design the content of a documentary film script and then they present and apply it as a film-showing event in class by inviting other students as protectors, activists, or people who give harm to endangered animals. The assignment will be evaluated by using rubrics.
EK_ALANLAR.Farklılaştırma:
Expansion
Objective: To talk about endangered animals and conservation efforts in English by using the target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 1: Digital Role-Play: Save an Endangered Animal
Students work in small groups and choose or are assigned an endangered animal (e.g., (Antalya) Caretta caretta turtles or Anatolian leopards). Using a web tool, they create a digital character or visual story that introduces the animal, its habitat, and the problems it faces (such as pollution or habitat loss). The animal ''speaks'' using recorded audio or text-to-speech to describe its challenges and suggest solutions. Groups present their digital work to the class while others take notes and give feedback on vocabulary, fluency, and presentation skills. After all presentations, the class holds a brainstorming session to discuss ideas for protecting the animals, using phrases like ''Every little bit helps!'' and ''We need to act now!''. The teacher provides feedback on the presentations, and students finish with a clear plan of actions and solutions. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.
Objective: To identify endangered animals and conservation efforts in English by using the target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 2: Collaborative Reading Puzzle: Endangered Animals
The teacher divides a complex reading text about endangered animals (e.g., caretta caretta turtles, Anatolian leopards) into sections, each with unique information (like habitat, threats, or solutions). Students work in small groups, and each group reads one section, identifying key points and preparing questions about missing information they need from other groups. After reading, groups take turns asking and answering questions to complete the full picture of the topic (e.g., ''What is threatening the Anatolian leopard?''). Once they gather all the information, each group presents a summary of their findings, combining what they read and learned from others. The class ends with a discussion on solutions to protect endangered animals. The teacher gives feedback on reading comprehension, vocabulary use, and collaboration throughout the activity. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.
Supporting
Objective: To describe endangered animals, their habitats, and ways to protect them from extinction in English by using the target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 1: Endangered Animal Habitat Matching Game
The teacher provides students with two sets of cards: one set with endangered animals (e.g., polar bear, sea turtle) and another with habitats (e.g., ocean, rainforest). Students work in pairs to match the animals with their correct habitats (e.g., Polar bear-Arctic). Once matched, they create simple sentences following the models on the board, such as ''A polar bear lives in the ocean'' or ''A tiger lives in the jungle'', and practice saying them aloud to improve pronunciation. The pair that completes the matches and sentences correctly and the fastest wins the game. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.
Objective: To identify endangered animals and their habitats in English by using target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 2: Endangered Animals Gap-Fill and Pronunciation Practice
The teacher starts by providing a short reading or audio about endangered animals like (Antalya) Caretta caretta sea turtles or Anatolian leopards. Students learn about their habitats, challenges, and ways to protect them. Afterward, students use the Web 2.00 tool to complete a gap-fill exercise with sentences such as ''A Caretta caretta turtle lays eggs on the (Mediterranean coast)''. After completing the exercise, students read their sentences aloud to practise pronunciation. The teacher then provides feedback on their accuracy and fluency.
The activity ends with a class discussion on protecting animals, using phrases like ''Every little bit helps!'' and ''It’s not too late to act!''. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.

plan.KONU:
Sub-themes: “Films, film genres, futuristic films with futuristic ideas, and technology”
Target Vocabulary in Use (with revisional vocabulary)
Vocabulary for film genres
Nouns: Film (movie-AmE), comedy, action, cartoon (animated-AmE), romantic (romance-AmE), family film, adventure, science fiction, detective film, historical film, thriller, mystery, horror, musical, documentary, biographical, crime, martial arts.
Vocabulary for futuristic film genres
Nouns: Space adventure, robots, alien invasion, time travel, time loop, space exploration, adventure, superheroes, science (sci-fi) fantasy, an invention, a discovery, a survival, an actor, an actress, a director, a crew, virtual reality, a myth. Verbs: To discover, to explore, to invent, to adapt, to control, to be into sth. Adjectives: Futuristic, robotic, artificial, virtual, technological, horrific, world-saving, legendary, global, optimistic, intelligent, epic.
*National and religious days, festivals and celebrations
“29 October Republic Day”, “23 April National Sovereignty and Children’s Day”, “19 May Commemoration of Atatürk, Youth and Sports Day”, “15 July Democracy and National Unity Day”, “30 August Victory Day”, "Eid al- Fitr (Eid-al-Ramadan)", "Festival of Sacrifice (Eid-al-Adha)".
*
(Relevant language content and (communicative) activities related to these national and religious days, festivals and celebrations will be developed and integrated across all themes and in all appropriate sections wherever and whenever possible.)
*
Local Cultural, Social and Moral Considerations of the Theme
In this theme, specific examples, cases, situations, events, and practices reflecting Turkish social, cultural, and moral customs, traditions, and heritage will be included across all sub-topics. This consideration will be age-and-level appropriate and selected with the Turkish learners’ social and cultural context in mind. A table of contents for this section is provided in the introduction to the whole English Language Curriculum.
Background Grammatical Structures in Use
-
The Simple Present Tense: (Adventure films show exciting places and happening.)
*About “Background Grammatical Structures in Use”
The “Background Grammatical Structures” in this section are not only revisional but also serve as contextual support and contribute to meaning-making. They are intended to be used within the theme to help students grasp the meaning of the language constructed through the use of “Target Grammatical Structures” without being explicitly taught. These structures are not considered “Target Grammatical Structures” themselves rather they function as a part of the facilitation process, supporting both the target forms and the contexts in which they are used. They provide opportunities for learning through revised and scaffolded language.
Target Grammatical Structures in Use
-
The Simple Future Tense (Positive, negative, Interrogative): (What (do you think) will happen in the future? (I think) robots will help people in the future. People will travel to other planets. Scientists will invent new machines to explore space. Time travellers will change history. People will live in virtual reality worlds.)
Functions of the Target Grammatical Structures in Use
-
Use of the Simple Present Tense: Describing events and happenings (in films).
-
Use of the Simple Future Tense: Describing predictions, expressing what speakers believe and expect, explaining speakers’ opinions or guesses about the future, describing advice, recommendations (and expectations).
Target Social Language Expressions in Use
This (film) is a breath of fresh air! This (film) is not my cup of tea!
I’m not brave enough to watch this! What’s next?
Target Phonological Sounds in Use
Diphthong: o, oe, owoa, ou, eau: /əʊ/ Consonants: y: (/j/, /i/; z: (/z/)
*
(Phonetic symbols will not be taught. Only sounds will be practised through the target words in the theme.)

EK_ALANLAR.Farklılaştırma:
Expansion
Objective: To talk about endangered animals and conservation efforts in English by using the target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 1: Digital Role-Play: Save an Endangered Animal
Students work in small groups and choose or are assigned an endangered animal (e.g., (Antalya) Caretta caretta turtles or Anatolian leopards). Using a web tool, they create a digital character or visual story that introduces the animal, its habitat, and the problems it faces (such as pollution or habitat loss). The animal ''speaks'' using recorded audio or text-to-speech to describe its challenges and suggest solutions. Groups present their digital work to the class while others take notes and give feedback on vocabulary, fluency, and presentation skills. After all presentations, the class holds a brainstorming session to discuss ideas for protecting the animals, using phrases like ''Every little bit helps!'' and ''We need to act now!''. The teacher provides feedback on the presentations, and students finish with a clear plan of actions and solutions. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.
Objective: To identify endangered animals and conservation efforts in English by using the target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 2: Collaborative Reading Puzzle: Endangered Animals
The teacher divides a complex reading text about endangered animals (e.g., caretta caretta turtles, Anatolian leopards) into sections, each with unique information (like habitat, threats, or solutions). Students work in small groups, and each group reads one section, identifying key points and preparing questions about missing information they need from other groups. After reading, groups take turns asking and answering questions to complete the full picture of the topic (e.g., ''What is threatening the Anatolian leopard?''). Once they gather all the information, each group presents a summary of their findings, combining what they read and learned from others. The class ends with a discussion on solutions to protect endangered animals. The teacher gives feedback on reading comprehension, vocabulary use, and collaboration throughout the activity. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.
Supporting
Objective: To describe endangered animals, their habitats, and ways to protect them from extinction in English by using the target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 1: Endangered Animal Habitat Matching Game
The teacher provides students with two sets of cards: one set with endangered animals (e.g., polar bear, sea turtle) and another with habitats (e.g., ocean, rainforest). Students work in pairs to match the animals with their correct habitats (e.g., Polar bear-Arctic). Once matched, they create simple sentences following the models on the board, such as ''A polar bear lives in the ocean'' or ''A tiger lives in the jungle'', and practice saying them aloud to improve pronunciation. The pair that completes the matches and sentences correctly and the fastest wins the game. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.
Objective: To identify endangered animals and their habitats in English by using target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 2: Endangered Animals Gap-Fill and Pronunciation Practice
The teacher starts by providing a short reading or audio about endangered animals like (Antalya) Caretta caretta sea turtles or Anatolian leopards. Students learn about their habitats, challenges, and ways to protect them. Afterward, students use the Web 2.00 tool to complete a gap-fill exercise with sentences such as ''A Caretta caretta turtle lays eggs on the (Mediterranean coast)''. After completing the exercise, students read their sentences aloud to practise pronunciation. The teacher then provides feedback on their accuracy and fluency.
The activity ends with a class discussion on protecting animals, using phrases like ''Every little bit helps!'' and ''It’s not too late to act!''. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.

plan.KONU:
Sub-themes: “Films, film genres, futuristic films with futuristic ideas, and technology”
Target Vocabulary in Use (with revisional vocabulary)
Vocabulary for film genres
Nouns: Film (movie-AmE), comedy, action, cartoon (animated-AmE), romantic (romance-AmE), family film, adventure, science fiction, detective film, historical film, thriller, mystery, horror, musical, documentary, biographical, crime, martial arts.
Vocabulary for futuristic film genres
Nouns: Space adventure, robots, alien invasion, time travel, time loop, space exploration, adventure, superheroes, science (sci-fi) fantasy, an invention, a discovery, a survival, an actor, an actress, a director, a crew, virtual reality, a myth. Verbs: To discover, to explore, to invent, to adapt, to control, to be into sth. Adjectives: Futuristic, robotic, artificial, virtual, technological, horrific, world-saving, legendary, global, optimistic, intelligent, epic.
*National and religious days, festivals and celebrations
“29 October Republic Day”, “23 April National Sovereignty and Children’s Day”, “19 May Commemoration of Atatürk, Youth and Sports Day”, “15 July Democracy and National Unity Day”, “30 August Victory Day”, "Eid al- Fitr (Eid-al-Ramadan)", "Festival of Sacrifice (Eid-al-Adha)".
*
(Relevant language content and (communicative) activities related to these national and religious days, festivals and celebrations will be developed and integrated across all themes and in all appropriate sections wherever and whenever possible.)
*
Local Cultural, Social and Moral Considerations of the Theme
In this theme, specific examples, cases, situations, events, and practices reflecting Turkish social, cultural, and moral customs, traditions, and heritage will be included across all sub-topics. This consideration will be age-and-level appropriate and selected with the Turkish learners’ social and cultural context in mind. A table of contents for this section is provided in the introduction to the whole English Language Curriculum.
Background Grammatical Structures in Use
-
The Simple Present Tense: (Adventure films show exciting places and happening.)
*About “Background Grammatical Structures in Use”
The “Background Grammatical Structures” in this section are not only revisional but also serve as contextual support and contribute to meaning-making. They are intended to be used within the theme to help students grasp the meaning of the language constructed through the use of “Target Grammatical Structures” without being explicitly taught. These structures are not considered “Target Grammatical Structures” themselves rather they function as a part of the facilitation process, supporting both the target forms and the contexts in which they are used. They provide opportunities for learning through revised and scaffolded language.
Target Grammatical Structures in Use
-
The Simple Future Tense (Positive, negative, Interrogative): (What (do you think) will happen in the future? (I think) robots will help people in the future. People will travel to other planets. Scientists will invent new machines to explore space. Time travellers will change history. People will live in virtual reality worlds.)
Functions of the Target Grammatical Structures in Use
-
Use of the Simple Present Tense: Describing events and happenings (in films).
-
Use of the Simple Future Tense: Describing predictions, expressing what speakers believe and expect, explaining speakers’ opinions or guesses about the future, describing advice, recommendations (and expectations).
Target Social Language Expressions in Use
This (film) is a breath of fresh air! This (film) is not my cup of tea!
I’m not brave enough to watch this! What’s next?
Target Phonological Sounds in Use
Diphthong: o, oe, owoa, ou, eau: /əʊ/ Consonants: y: (/j/, /i/; z: (/z/)
*
(Phonetic symbols will not be taught. Only sounds will be practised through the target words in the theme.)

EK_ALANLAR.Farklılaştırma:
Expansion
Objective: To talk about endangered animals and conservation efforts in English by using the target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 1: Digital Role-Play: Save an Endangered Animal
Students work in small groups and choose or are assigned an endangered animal (e.g., (Antalya) Caretta caretta turtles or Anatolian leopards). Using a web tool, they create a digital character or visual story that introduces the animal, its habitat, and the problems it faces (such as pollution or habitat loss). The animal ''speaks'' using recorded audio or text-to-speech to describe its challenges and suggest solutions. Groups present their digital work to the class while others take notes and give feedback on vocabulary, fluency, and presentation skills. After all presentations, the class holds a brainstorming session to discuss ideas for protecting the animals, using phrases like ''Every little bit helps!'' and ''We need to act now!''. The teacher provides feedback on the presentations, and students finish with a clear plan of actions and solutions. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.
Objective: To identify endangered animals and conservation efforts in English by using the target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 2: Collaborative Reading Puzzle: Endangered Animals
The teacher divides a complex reading text about endangered animals (e.g., caretta caretta turtles, Anatolian leopards) into sections, each with unique information (like habitat, threats, or solutions). Students work in small groups, and each group reads one section, identifying key points and preparing questions about missing information they need from other groups. After reading, groups take turns asking and answering questions to complete the full picture of the topic (e.g., ''What is threatening the Anatolian leopard?''). Once they gather all the information, each group presents a summary of their findings, combining what they read and learned from others. The class ends with a discussion on solutions to protect endangered animals. The teacher gives feedback on reading comprehension, vocabulary use, and collaboration throughout the activity. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.
Supporting
Objective: To describe endangered animals, their habitats, and ways to protect them from extinction in English by using the target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 1: Endangered Animal Habitat Matching Game
The teacher provides students with two sets of cards: one set with endangered animals (e.g., polar bear, sea turtle) and another with habitats (e.g., ocean, rainforest). Students work in pairs to match the animals with their correct habitats (e.g., Polar bear-Arctic). Once matched, they create simple sentences following the models on the board, such as ''A polar bear lives in the ocean'' or ''A tiger lives in the jungle'', and practice saying them aloud to improve pronunciation. The pair that completes the matches and sentences correctly and the fastest wins the game. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.
Objective: To identify endangered animals and their habitats in English by using target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 2: Endangered Animals Gap-Fill and Pronunciation Practice
The teacher starts by providing a short reading or audio about endangered animals like (Antalya) Caretta caretta sea turtles or Anatolian leopards. Students learn about their habitats, challenges, and ways to protect them. Afterward, students use the Web 2.00 tool to complete a gap-fill exercise with sentences such as ''A Caretta caretta turtle lays eggs on the (Mediterranean coast)''. After completing the exercise, students read their sentences aloud to practise pronunciation. The teacher then provides feedback on their accuracy and fluency.
The activity ends with a class discussion on protecting animals, using phrases like ''Every little bit helps!'' and ''It’s not too late to act!''. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.

plan.ÜNİTE: THEME 8: LIFE IN THE UNIVERSE & FUTURE
plan.KONU:
Sub-themes: “Films, film genres, futuristic films with futuristic ideas, and technology”
Target Vocabulary in Use (with revisional vocabulary)
Vocabulary for film genres
Nouns: Film (movie-AmE), comedy, action, cartoon (animated-AmE), romantic (romance-AmE), family film, adventure, science fiction, detective film, historical film, thriller, mystery, horror, musical, documentary, biographical, crime, martial arts.
Vocabulary for futuristic film genres
Nouns: Space adventure, robots, alien invasion, time travel, time loop, space exploration, adventure, superheroes, science (sci-fi) fantasy, an invention, a discovery, a survival, an actor, an actress, a director, a crew, virtual reality, a myth. Verbs: To discover, to explore, to invent, to adapt, to control, to be into sth. Adjectives: Futuristic, robotic, artificial, virtual, technological, horrific, world-saving, legendary, global, optimistic, intelligent, epic.
*National and religious days, festivals and celebrations
“29 October Republic Day”, “23 April National Sovereignty and Children’s Day”, “19 May Commemoration of Atatürk, Youth and Sports Day”, “15 July Democracy and National Unity Day”, “30 August Victory Day”, "Eid al- Fitr (Eid-al-Ramadan)", "Festival of Sacrifice (Eid-al-Adha)".
*
(Relevant language content and (communicative) activities related to these national and religious days, festivals and celebrations will be developed and integrated across all themes and in all appropriate sections wherever and whenever possible.)
*
Local Cultural, Social and Moral Considerations of the Theme
In this theme, specific examples, cases, situations, events, and practices reflecting Turkish social, cultural, and moral customs, traditions, and heritage will be included across all sub-topics. This consideration will be age-and-level appropriate and selected with the Turkish learners’ social and cultural context in mind. A table of contents for this section is provided in the introduction to the whole English Language Curriculum.
Background Grammatical Structures in Use
-
The Simple Present Tense: (Adventure films show exciting places and happening.)
*About “Background Grammatical Structures in Use”
The “Background Grammatical Structures” in this section are not only revisional but also serve as contextual support and contribute to meaning-making. They are intended to be used within the theme to help students grasp the meaning of the language constructed through the use of “Target Grammatical Structures” without being explicitly taught. These structures are not considered “Target Grammatical Structures” themselves rather they function as a part of the facilitation process, supporting both the target forms and the contexts in which they are used. They provide opportunities for learning through revised and scaffolded language.
Target Grammatical Structures in Use
-
The Simple Future Tense (Positive, negative, Interrogative): (What (do you think) will happen in the future? (I think) robots will help people in the future. People will travel to other planets. Scientists will invent new machines to explore space. Time travellers will change history. People will live in virtual reality worlds.)
Functions of the Target Grammatical Structures in Use
-
Use of the Simple Present Tense: Describing events and happenings (in films).
-
Use of the Simple Future Tense: Describing predictions, expressing what speakers believe and expect, explaining speakers’ opinions or guesses about the future, describing advice, recommendations (and expectations).
Target Social Language Expressions in Use
This (film) is a breath of fresh air! This (film) is not my cup of tea!
I’m not brave enough to watch this! What’s next?
Target Phonological Sounds in Use
Diphthong: o, oe, owoa, ou, eau: /əʊ/ Consonants: y: (/j/, /i/; z: (/z/)
*
(Phonetic symbols will not be taught. Only sounds will be practised through the target words in the theme.)

EK_ALANLAR.Ölçme: PERFORMANCE ASSIGNMENT:They write and design the content of a futuristic film script and then they present and apply it as a film-showing event in class by inviting other students as actors, actresses, directors etc. The assignment will be evaluated by using rubrics.
EK_ALANLAR.Farklılaştırma:
Expansion
Objective: To talk about futuristic films in English by using the target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 1: Futuristic Film Promotion
In this activity, students work in small groups and brainstorm a futuristic film idea, including the genre (e.g., time travel), plot (e.g., robots saving or harming humanity), and characters (e.g., an adventurous crew). Each group collaborates to develop and present their film promotion to the class. They use descriptive adjectives such as futuristic, advanced, technological to enhance their presentation. As a final product, students design a poster that displays their film idea, featuring its title, key elements, and visuals to represent their concept. After each presentation, the teacher and peers give constructive feedback, focusing on creativity, use of target vocabulary, and clarity of ideas. They also provide positive reinforcement feedback to help students refine their language and teamwork skills. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.
Objective: To help students reconstruct a futuristic film concept in English through an interactive information gap activity by using the target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 2: Reconstructing the Film Schema
In this activity, students work in groups and are provided with different parts of a text describing a futuristic film (e.g., the plot, characters, and futuristic elements such as space exploration or advanced technology). Each group member receives a unique section of the text to read individually. One student from the group stands at the board to create a film schema, including elements like the title, main plot, characters, and key futuristic themes.
Group members, after reading their parts, explain the information to the student at the board in their own words, ensuring they use the target vocabulary such as futuristic, advanced, technological and the target grammar where appropriate (e.g., ''The film will focus on robots saving humanity''.2). The student at the board uses the shared information to fill in the schema.
In the end, the teacher reveals the original film schema, and the class compares it to the reconstructed version. The groups discuss the differences and provide feedback on the accuracy and clarity of their communication. The teacher and peers give constructive feedback, highlighting effective explanations, use of vocabulary, and teamwork, while offering suggestions for improvement. This activity ensures active participation and collaborative learning while fostering critical thinking and language development. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.
supporint
Objective: To help students describe different film genres in English by using the target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 1: Film Genre Match-Up
In this activity, students receive a worksheet containing film genre names such as comedy, action, time travel, and space adventure alongside images representing each genre. They match each image with the correct genre name, helping them associate vocabulary with visual cues. To reinforce support and enhance their understanding, students write one sentence about their favourite genre by using target language items, for example, ''Comedy films make people laugh''. A word bank with genre names and sample sentences is provided to guide them. At the end of the activity, students actively share their sentences with the class or in small groups, fostering engagement and allowing them to practice the target vocabulary. After sharing, the teacher and peers provide feedback, focusing on sentence accuracy, use of target vocabulary, and creativity. Positive reinforcement is used to encourage participation and highlight successful language use, helping students to build confidence and improve their skills. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.
Objective: To talk about futuristic ideas in English by using the target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 2: Futuristic Sentence Builder
In this activity, students are provided with sentence fragments on physical cards (e.g., ''Robots will'', ''help people'', ''in the future'') or digital cards using web 2.0 tools if available. Students rearrange the fragments to create meaningful and grammatically correct sentences, focusing on futuristic ideas. For those without access to web 2.0 tools, teachers can distribute printed sentence fragments or write them on the board for group work. Visual aids such as printed or drawn pictures of robots, space exploration, and alien invasions can be used to stimulate ideas.
After students create their sentences, they read them aloud to the class or in small groups. The teacher and peers provide constructive feedback, focusing on accuracy, creativity, and use of target vocabulary. Positive reinforcement is encouraged to build confidence and highlight successful usage of the target language. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.

plan.ÜNİTE: THEME 8: LIFE IN THE UNIVERSE & FUTURE
plan.KONU:
Sub-themes: “Films, film genres, futuristic films with futuristic ideas, and technology”
Target Vocabulary in Use (with revisional vocabulary)
Vocabulary for film genres
Nouns: Film (movie-AmE), comedy, action, cartoon (animated-AmE), romantic (romance-AmE), family film, adventure, science fiction, detective film, historical film, thriller, mystery, horror, musical, documentary, biographical, crime, martial arts.
Vocabulary for futuristic film genres
Nouns: Space adventure, robots, alien invasion, time travel, time loop, space exploration, adventure, superheroes, science (sci-fi) fantasy, an invention, a discovery, a survival, an actor, an actress, a director, a crew, virtual reality, a myth. Verbs: To discover, to explore, to invent, to adapt, to control, to be into sth. Adjectives: Futuristic, robotic, artificial, virtual, technological, horrific, world-saving, legendary, global, optimistic, intelligent, epic.
*National and religious days, festivals and celebrations
“29 October Republic Day”, “23 April National Sovereignty and Children’s Day”, “19 May Commemoration of Atatürk, Youth and Sports Day”, “15 July Democracy and National Unity Day”, “30 August Victory Day”, "Eid al- Fitr (Eid-al-Ramadan)", "Festival of Sacrifice (Eid-al-Adha)".
*
(Relevant language content and (communicative) activities related to these national and religious days, festivals and celebrations will be developed and integrated across all themes and in all appropriate sections wherever and whenever possible.)
*
Local Cultural, Social and Moral Considerations of the Theme
In this theme, specific examples, cases, situations, events, and practices reflecting Turkish social, cultural, and moral customs, traditions, and heritage will be included across all sub-topics. This consideration will be age-and-level appropriate and selected with the Turkish learners’ social and cultural context in mind. A table of contents for this section is provided in the introduction to the whole English Language Curriculum.
Background Grammatical Structures in Use
-
The Simple Present Tense: (Adventure films show exciting places and happening.)
*About “Background Grammatical Structures in Use”
The “Background Grammatical Structures” in this section are not only revisional but also serve as contextual support and contribute to meaning-making. They are intended to be used within the theme to help students grasp the meaning of the language constructed through the use of “Target Grammatical Structures” without being explicitly taught. These structures are not considered “Target Grammatical Structures” themselves rather they function as a part of the facilitation process, supporting both the target forms and the contexts in which they are used. They provide opportunities for learning through revised and scaffolded language.
Target Grammatical Structures in Use
-
The Simple Future Tense (Positive, negative, Interrogative): (What (do you think) will happen in the future? (I think) robots will help people in the future. People will travel to other planets. Scientists will invent new machines to explore space. Time travellers will change history. People will live in virtual reality worlds.)
Functions of the Target Grammatical Structures in Use
-
Use of the Simple Present Tense: Describing events and happenings (in films).
-
Use of the Simple Future Tense: Describing predictions, expressing what speakers believe and expect, explaining speakers’ opinions or guesses about the future, describing advice, recommendations (and expectations).
Target Social Language Expressions in Use
This (film) is a breath of fresh air! This (film) is not my cup of tea!
I’m not brave enough to watch this! What’s next?
Target Phonological Sounds in Use
Diphthong: o, oe, owoa, ou, eau: /əʊ/ Consonants: y: (/j/, /i/; z: (/z/)
*
(Phonetic symbols will not be taught. Only sounds will be practised through the target words in the theme.)

School-based planning includes research and observation, social activities, project work, local studies, reading activities, and similar tasks that are decided to be carried out within the scope of the course by the subject teachers’ board. The time allocated for these activities is scheduled within the academic year and expressed in the annual plans. EK_ALANLAR.Ölçme: PERFORMANCE ASSIGNMENT:They write and design the content of a futuristic film script and then they present and apply it as a film-showing event in class by inviting other students as actors, actresses, directors etc. The assignment will be evaluated by using rubrics.
EK_ALANLAR.Farklılaştırma:
Expansion
Objective: To talk about futuristic films in English by using the target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 1: Futuristic Film Promotion
In this activity, students work in small groups and brainstorm a futuristic film idea, including the genre (e.g., time travel), plot (e.g., robots saving or harming humanity), and characters (e.g., an adventurous crew). Each group collaborates to develop and present their film promotion to the class. They use descriptive adjectives such as futuristic, advanced, technological to enhance their presentation. As a final product, students design a poster that displays their film idea, featuring its title, key elements, and visuals to represent their concept. After each presentation, the teacher and peers give constructive feedback, focusing on creativity, use of target vocabulary, and clarity of ideas. They also provide positive reinforcement feedback to help students refine their language and teamwork skills. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.
Objective: To help students reconstruct a futuristic film concept in English through an interactive information gap activity by using the target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 2: Reconstructing the Film Schema
In this activity, students work in groups and are provided with different parts of a text describing a futuristic film (e.g., the plot, characters, and futuristic elements such as space exploration or advanced technology). Each group member receives a unique section of the text to read individually. One student from the group stands at the board to create a film schema, including elements like the title, main plot, characters, and key futuristic themes.
Group members, after reading their parts, explain the information to the student at the board in their own words, ensuring they use the target vocabulary such as futuristic, advanced, technological and the target grammar where appropriate (e.g., ''The film will focus on robots saving humanity''.2). The student at the board uses the shared information to fill in the schema.
In the end, the teacher reveals the original film schema, and the class compares it to the reconstructed version. The groups discuss the differences and provide feedback on the accuracy and clarity of their communication. The teacher and peers give constructive feedback, highlighting effective explanations, use of vocabulary, and teamwork, while offering suggestions for improvement. This activity ensures active participation and collaborative learning while fostering critical thinking and language development. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.
supporint
Objective: To help students describe different film genres in English by using the target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 1: Film Genre Match-Up
In this activity, students receive a worksheet containing film genre names such as comedy, action, time travel, and space adventure alongside images representing each genre. They match each image with the correct genre name, helping them associate vocabulary with visual cues. To reinforce support and enhance their understanding, students write one sentence about their favourite genre by using target language items, for example, ''Comedy films make people laugh''. A word bank with genre names and sample sentences is provided to guide them. At the end of the activity, students actively share their sentences with the class or in small groups, fostering engagement and allowing them to practice the target vocabulary. After sharing, the teacher and peers provide feedback, focusing on sentence accuracy, use of target vocabulary, and creativity. Positive reinforcement is used to encourage participation and highlight successful language use, helping students to build confidence and improve their skills. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.
Objective: To talk about futuristic ideas in English by using the target vocabulary and target grammar.
Activity 2: Futuristic Sentence Builder
In this activity, students are provided with sentence fragments on physical cards (e.g., ''Robots will'', ''help people'', ''in the future'') or digital cards using web 2.0 tools if available. Students rearrange the fragments to create meaningful and grammatically correct sentences, focusing on futuristic ideas. For those without access to web 2.0 tools, teachers can distribute printed sentence fragments or write them on the board for group work. Visual aids such as printed or drawn pictures of robots, space exploration, and alien invasions can be used to stimulate ideas.
After students create their sentences, they read them aloud to the class or in small groups. The teacher and peers provide constructive feedback, focusing on accuracy, creativity, and use of target vocabulary. Positive reinforcement is encouraged to build confidence and highlight successful usage of the target language. Students reflect on their thoughts and feelings about the activity.
